summary.intent: Investigate and fix a failing CI E2E test in writable-shares.spec.ts where breadcrumbs didn't update after navigating into a nested subfolder created by a write-share recipient.
summary.outcome: Identified and fixed two bugs: (1) the API's addShareKeys endpoint incorrectly blocked write-share recipients from adding 'folder' type keys for subfolders they create, and (2) an E2E test race condition where navigation completion wasn't properly awaited. PR #374 was created and review comments were resolved.

repo: Write-share recipient subfolder keys (folder, folder-ipns) are stored in share_keys table; the root folder key lives in the shares table itself — so restricting folder-type keys in share_keys was overly broad.
navigateToSubfolder in useSharedNavigation.ts has a catch block that swallows errors with console.warn, displaying 'Failed to open subfolder' in the UI but not surfacing the error to callers.
The API runs with NODE_ENV=development locally which enforces rate limiting; CI uses NODE_ENV=test which relaxes throttle limits — mixing these breaks auth (Web3Auth) and causes 429s.
The writable-shares E2E tests are fully serial — tests 8.x depend on earlier phases (1.x account creation, share setup) so individual tests cannot be run in isolation.
The api-client package must be rebuilt after branch switches if new endpoints were added; stale builds cause blank-page JS import errors in the web app.

code.finding: Overly broad guard blocked write-share recipients from adding any 'folder' keyType keys, including for subfolders they legitimately create. The fix removes this restriction so recipients can add subfolder keys.
Added navigateIntoSubfolder(name) method that double-clicks a folder and awaits breadcrumb update (toContainText with 30s timeout) to prove async navigation completed before the test proceeds.

navigateToSubfolder is async (IPNS resolution + key unwrapping + metadata decryption). The old test pattern waited on parentDirRow visibility which was already true, causing a race condition on slow CI.

workflow: Screenshots in test-results/*/test-failed-N.png are the primary debugging tool for E2E failures — UI error messages rendered in the app are visible there.
Playwright error-context.md only captures the page context of the test's primary actor (Alice), not secondary browser contexts (Bob) — so errors on Bob's page require reading screenshots.
Adding temporary console.error with detailed messages to catch blocks is an effective local debugging technique for swallowed async errors in hooks.
1Password SSH signing requires an active desktop session — commits from terminal sessions where the agent isn't available will fail; must retry when desktop is active.

friction: Local E2E run initially failed with blank page because the api-client package was stale after branch switch — required full package rebuild before tests could run.
NODE_ENV=development causes rate limiting (429) that blocks E2E tests locally; NODE_ENV=test breaks Web3Auth initialization — no clean local equivalent of CI's environment.
navigateToSubfolder's silent catch block required adding temporary debug logging to identify the actual error ('No key available for this subfolder'), which wasn't surfaced anywhere.
1Password SSH agent unavailable during commit attempt required user to return from AFK before the commit could proceed.
Serial E2E test structure means the full suite (~8 phases) must run even to test a Phase 8 fix, making iteration slow.
The stash created during branch switch reverted code changes, requiring all edits to be re-applied.
open_items: The SDK's addShareKeysFn catch block in createSharedSubfolder silently swallows errors with console.warn — should propagate so callers can handle failures rather than leaving orphaned folder metadata.
Local E2E environment parity with CI for rate limiting is unresolved — no documented way to run E2E tests locally without hitting 429s or breaking auth.

The navigateIntoSubfolder breadcrumb check uses toContainText which could theoretically match an ancestor crumb with the same name — CodeRabbit flagged this; exact-match assertion would be more robust.
